### Title: Pretend It’s the Last Time

### Content: 
My sister once reminded me that there are plenty of last times we miss. The last time we hang out with a friend before our paths twist in separate directions. The last time we have a certain food before we leave a place we’ll never revisit. Sometimes, we might even fail to recognize the last phone call with someone we love before they die. That’s why “this might be the last time” is a thought worth having on occasion.
It’t a thought to have all the time. If you did, you’d be paralyzed. It’s not the kind of idea you can hold on to. You can only drop it in your brain and see where it lands. Let it rest for a while. Then, it will make its way. You’ll be reminded to call your friend. You’ll eat a certain dish at a certain restaurant. You’ll take a picture of your grandfather while he’s asleep.
The idea is to remember without remembering. To allow the thought to do its work without forcing it. That’s what I’m doing right now. I’m not trying to make you do anything. I’m just writing. You’re just reading. And yet, if you think about it, this might be the last time you read one of my posts.
You can’t know, of course. But it’s a possibility. And if it’s the last time, I want you to know that I’m grateful. Grateful you came here. Grateful you read my writing. Grateful you spent some of your time with me. And if you never come back, I’ll be sad, but I’ll also be happy. Happy that I got to write this post. Happy that I got to say thank you. Happy that I got to pretend it was the last time.

### Title: Flick It Again

### Content: 
We have a big cuddle blanket on our couch. It’s massive. Two by two meters or so. In the winter, we use it every night, and every morning, I fold it back into shape.
To’t fold a blanket properly. You have to flick it. The right amount of momentum will allow you to fold it in half, and then in half again, and then in half again. Until you have a neat little package that fits back into its place.
I’ve been folding blankets for over 30 years, and yet, I still have to flick it again. The first flick is never enough. It’s always the second one that gets the blanket to fold neatly. It’s a good reminder: Don’t be afraid to flick it again. To try once more. To give it another go. You might have to do it two, three, four times, but eventually, you’ll get there.
Whether it’s a blanket, a project, or a relationship, don’t be afraid to flick it again.

### Title: Appreciate the Basics

### Content: 
Today, our apartment has no water for eight hours. The irony? Outside, it’s raining all day long. But there’s a difference between water coming out of the sky or the ground and fresh H2O pouring out of your tap, and you only realize how big of a difference it is when you’re left without your usual conveniences.
Couldand you fill it with water from the rain, it’ll be a different kind of water than the kind you usually drink. It’s less filtered, less processed, and it’s also less safe to drink. It’s also a lot of work to collect, and you’ll have to boil it to make it safe. That’s a lot of steps for something that, usually, just flows effortlessly from your tap.
It’s easy to forget how much we depend on the basics when we have them. We don’t think about the water we drink, the food we eat, and the electricity we use. We don’t think about the roads we drive on, the phones we talk on, and the internet we browse. But when any one of these things is taken away, we realize how much we depend on them.
The next time you turn on the tap and water comes out, take a moment to appreciate it. The next time you flick a switch and the lights come on, take a moment to appreciate it. The next time you open your fridge and see food, take a moment to appreciate it.
Appreciate the basics. They’re not so basic after all.

### Title: Nothing Is True, Everything Is Permitted

Thus goes the creed of the Assassins, a secret organization sworn to protect humanity’s ability to choose. Whereas the Templars would rather do away with free will and keep the world at peace by putting it to sleep, the Assassins insist on their right to make mistakes and live with the consequences—for better or for worse.
In innumerable battles across time and space, the two groups have fought for their ideals. They are the yin and yang of history, and their struggle is the theme of the video game series Assassin’s Creed, in which the player can relive the lives of several Assassins throughout history.
It is also a theme that, as it turns out, goes well beyond video games. It is a theme that runs through all of history. A theme that’s still alive and well today. A theme that can teach us a thing or two about life, if only we take a moment to stop and think about it.
Nothing is true, everything is permitted. It is the Assassins’ motto, and it’s a motto worth remembering. Why? Because it’s a reminder that, even though we don’t have all the answers, we still have the right to ask questions.
It’s a reminder that we can choose to see the world as a place full of wonder and mystery, instead of a place where everything is already decided and there’s nothing left to discover.
It’s a reminder that we can choose to be curious and open-minded, instead of closed off and set in our ways.
It’s a reminder that we can choose to be kind and compassionate, instead of judgmental and cruel.
It’s a reminder that we can choose to be optimistic and hopeful, instead of pessimistic and resigned.
It’s a reminder that we can choose to be happy and content, instead of miserable and unhappy.

### Title: Delete the Adjectives, Get the Facts

### Content: 
Cool-headed as she is, Scout Finch cannot escape every trap life sets for any child growing up with a four years older brother. By the time Jem hits sixth grade, he actually gets interested in what school has to offer. Unfortunately for Scout, whatever he learns he blows out of proportion when relaying it to her.
Did’t he know his sister is only in second grade? Or does he simply take pleasure in making her feel stupid? It is a mystery to this day. But one day, he comes home with a new word: “Nigger-lover.” He explains to Scout what it means, and she promptly uses it to insult their neighbor, a lawyer who is defending a black man in court. Atticus, their father, overhears the incident and teaches Scout a lesson she will never forget:
“Scout, you’ll get in trouble if you go around saying things like that. You want to grow up to be a lady, don’t you? Now I warned you about foul language. There’s been some high talk around town to the effect that I shouldn’t do anything that displeases the Cunningham’s. Do you know what a compromise is? No, honey. If you and I ever looked at any crowd of folks and thought they looked exactly like us, then a lot of them would have to be displaced persons and live in tents. Now, I don’t want you to get mixed up in any of that. I don’t want you fighting any more, I don’t want to see you with your head in a knot over it. Just remember this: what you do affects other people.”
“Like what?” “Like, what Atticus does is, he defends niggers. He likes ’em up to a point. But he says that folks are just plain stingy when it comes down to paying for it. Over here in Maycomb, if they want to pay two dollars for a good seat at the picture show, they’ll pay six and go help Mr. Cunningham out of a jam. But let Mr. Cunningham be in a tight and he’ll pay his own way. He’ll never take help from folks he thinks is beneath him.”
“Why is it all right to take help from folks we think is above us, but it’s not all right to take help from folks we think is beneath us?” “I don’t know, honey. Sometimes I think there’s just one kind of folks. Folks.”

### Title: A Circle of Teaching

### Content: 
Yesterday, I showed my fiancée a bratwurst stall that I used to go to as a child when we went shopping in a certain town. Fresh rolls, lightly charred sausages—still a classic! After the salesman handed over the goods, I looked around for ketchup and mustard. I conveniently found them beside the stall.
The’t was a small, old-fashioned stand. The kind that’s made out of wood and metal and only has a few knobs to control the temperature and flow of the sauce. I turned the ketchup knob, and nothing happened. I tried again, harder. Still nothing. I went to the mustard, and that didn’t work either. I turned both knobs a few times, but it seemed the machine was empty.
I walked back to my fiancée and said: “I don’t think it works. Let’s eat them without sauce.” “You can’t eat bratwurst without sauce!” she said. “You have to try again!” So I did. I turned the knobs some more, and then, lo and behold, a tiny drop of ketchup fell into the tray. I tried again, and this time, a small dollop of mustard came out. Success!
I was about to put the sauces on our rolls when my fiancée said: “You have to show me how it works!” I did, and then I told her: “You know, you can’t eat bratwurst without sauce.” “Yes, I do now!” she said. “Thank you for teaching me!”
That’s how life works. We learn from each other, and then we teach each other. It’s a never-ending circle, and it’s how we get to enjoy the best things in life. A bratwurst stall from our childhood, a new kind of sauce, or a new way of looking at the world. We’re all students and teachers, and we’re all here to share the best parts of our lives with one another.
Don’t forget to show someone how the sauce machine works.

### Title: The Humble Shooter

### Content: 
At one point in To Kill a Mockingbird, a dog with rabies slowly walks up to the house of our hero family, the Finches. After housekeeper Calpurnia promptly drags the kids, who discovered the threat, off the street, she calls for their dad, Atticus, to come home.
Soon, Atticus appears, and with him, Heck Tate, the town’s sheriff. The two men have a brief conversation, and then, Heck hands Atticus a gun. “Take him, Mr. Finch,” he says. Atticus is hesitant. “For God’s sake, Heck, can’t you get a dead shot?”
Heck, however, is not to be moved. “I can take out his hindquarters with this gun,” he says, pointing at his own rifle. “I can pound his head off with this,” and he points at his handgun. “But I just can’t shoot that well, Mr. Finch. I can’t begin to shoot well enough to anchor that dog. I tried to anchor him five times with my rifle and missed him every time. Look, I can shoot straight, but not good enough to kill him. Look, I’m just a coward, Mr. Finch. I’m just a low-down Maycomb nigger-lover, but I’m still a coward.”
Atticus is still reluctant, but Heck insists. “Mr. Finch, this is a one-shot job. He’s moving slow and he logs, but you can turn him into a varmint if you don’t put him down the first shot. You can’t afford to miss.”
Atticus takes the gun, and Heck tells him the dog is about 25 yards away. Atticus closes one eye and aims. The children are watching. “Don’t waste time, Mr. Finch,” Heck says. “God knows what he’s up to.”
Atticus takes the shot, and the dog drops dead. “Well, I’ll be damned,” Heck says. “He hit him just where I wanted him to.”
The children, however, are stunned. They had no idea their dad was such a good shot. “Atticus Finch? One-shot Finch? The deadest shot in Maycomb County?”
Atticus just shakes his head. “I haven’t shot a gun in thirty years,” he says. Heck, however, is proud. “I saw that, Mr. Finch. It was beautiful.” Atticus, however, is not happy. “It’s not time to learn it,” he says. “It’ll happen little by little, it always does.”
Heck insists. “I’m not much of a boy any more, but I’ll tell you one thing: you don’t have to worry about anything any more. I’ll tell everybody. I swear before God, Mr. Finch, I’ll tell everybody.”
“Don’t do that,” Atticus says. “Don’t say anything about it. It’d ruin him for life. It’d be the very thing he would want.”
The children are still in shock. “You’re the best shot in the county,” they say. Atticus, however, is not amused. “I haven’t held a rifle to my shoulder in thirty-five years, Mr. Finch, and if you thought I was going to back out of this you were mistaken.”
“Mr. Finch,” Heck says. “People just aren’t like that.”
Atticus just shakes his head. “You know, Heck,” he says. “I’ve got it in me to shoot all the bluejays on this side of the creek. But I can remember when all I wanted to do was shoot a bluejay. I guess the only thing I wanted to do then was show you I could shoot. I know I’m wrong, it’s been twenty years, but I still see him down the street every day of my life. I still hear his voice tonight.”
Atticus is talking about his dad, and his eyes are full of tears. “I see him as he walked away from me. I see him as he looked back at me. I hear him say, ‘I swear boy, sometimes you act so much like a girl.’”
Atticus wipes his tears. “Scout,” he says. “I’m nothin’ but a country lawyer on a street full of bankers and businessmen doing their best each day. It’s all I can do to keep up with my clients. I can’t afford to miss.”
Atticus hands the gun back to Heck. “I just wanted you to see what real courage is, instead of getting the idea that courage is a man with a gun in his hand. It’s when you know you’re licked before you begin but you begin anyway and you see it through no matter what. You rarely win, but sometimes you do. Mrs. Dubose won, all ninety-eight pounds of her. According to her views, she died beholden to nothing and nobody. She was the bravest person I ever knew.”
Atticus looks at his children. “I wanted you to see something about her—I wanted you to see what real courage is, instead of getting the idea that courage is a man with a gun in his hand. It’s when you know you’re licked before you begin but you begin anyway and you see it through no matter what. You rarely win, but sometimes you do.”
“Mr. Finch, there’s a lot of ugly things in this world, sometimes I feel so ashamed. I guess every man ought to learn what it feels like to be a nigger at least once. I mean actually be one for a day. It’s different somehow. Atticus, you ought to walk in their shoes for a day.”
Atticus is still sad. “I do it every day of my life.”
“Mr. Finch,” Heck says. “You’re a good man. You’re the same in the courtroom as you are on the public streets. That’s what my mother says about you.”
Atticus is not convinced. “You mean that from now on I’ll never be able to walk through the middle aisle of the First Baptist Church without the head deacon as ‘Good morning, Brother Finch?’”

When my new co-worker told me she loved the Berlin nightlife, I tried to remember the last time I went to a club. It took me a solid ten minutes. I realized I had even been to one last year during a bachelor party—but before then? No clue.
There’t even remember the last time I went to a club. I don’t miss it.
I’m 33, and I guess it’s normal to grow out of certain things. But the clubbing scene? That’s something I never really grew into. I went to my first club when I was 21, and I only went because it was the only place you could legally drink in the US. I was studying abroad in Texas, and I was a student, so I didn’t have much money. The clubs were cheap, and the beer was free. The music was loud, the people were sweaty, and it was all a bit too much.
But I went, and I had fun. I met new people, and I learned how to dance. I even had a few flings. But after a while, I started to realize that I didn’t really enjoy it. I didn’t like the music, I didn’t like the crowds, and I didn’t like the fact that I had to shout to be heard.
So I stopped going. I found other ways to have fun. I went to bars, I went to concerts, and I went to parties. I even started hosting my own parties. I had a great time, and I didn’t miss the clubs at all.
Now, 12 years later, I’m a different person. I’m married, I have a job, and I have a house. I don’t go out as much as I used to, and I don’t drink as much as I used to. But I still have fun. I still go to bars, I still go to concerts, and I still go to parties. I just don’t go to clubs.

Here’s to growing up and finding your own path. Cheers!

### Title: Good People

### Content: 
Those are the ones we seek, aren’t they? But what does “good” mean? Three examples, one lesson.
Yesterday,, three examples, one lesson.
When my girlfriend and I visited a restaurant, the waiter gave us the usual spiel: “We have this, we have that, we have that, and we have this.” Then, he said: “And we also have a dish with pork belly, but it’s not on the menu, and I don’t recommend it. It’s not very good. You should get one of the other dishes.”
The waiter had no reason to say that. He could have tried to sell us the pork belly dish. He could have pretended it was a great dish. He could have stayed quiet. Instead, he told us the truth. He told us what was best for us, not what was best for him.
Good people give you the truth when it matters.
A few weeks ago, I had a problem with my tax return. I called the hotline, and a man answered. He explained the situation to me and said: “This is what happened. This is what we did. This is what you need to do.”
Then, he said: “I can see you’re not happy. I’m sorry. But this is the process. If you don’t do it, you’ll get a reminder. If you don’t do it then, you’ll get a fine. I’m sorry. I wish I could do more for you. But this is the process. I hope you have a good day.”
Good people apologize when it matters.
When I was in high school, I had a teacher who taught us about the Holocaust. He had been to Auschwitz, and he showed us pictures. He told us stories. He made us understand the magnitude of it. The scale of it. The humanity of it.
He also told us that, after the war, there was a big trial in Nuremberg, where the people who had been responsible for it were brought to justice. Then, he said: “But you know what? I don’t think any of them were really guilty. I think they were just people like you and me. They were just trying to survive. They were just trying to do their job. They were just trying to get through the day. And then, they woke up one day, and they were in hell. I don’t think any of them were really guilty. I think they were just people like you and me.”
Good people make you understand when it matters.
Good people tell you the truth, and they apologize when they can’t. Good people help you understand, and they don’t judge you for it. Good people are the ones we seek, and they’re the only ones worth seeking.
Look for good people.

Based’t know, but my friend is a hardcore dark chocolate fan. 70% cocoa and above. He can’t stand anything else. “It’s just too sweet,” he says. And yet, he brought me milk chocolate.
“Maybe it’s not that sweet?” I wondered. As it turns out, it’s not. I think it’s the best milk chocolate I’ve ever had. Not too sweet, not too bitter. A perfect balance of flavors. It’s also not cheap. At 12 euros for 100 grams, it’s more expensive than even the most expensive Lindt chocolate.
As I was chewing on a piece, however, I realized: “It’s still chocolate. It’s still the same product. Just a different version of it.” And while I can see why someone might pay 12 euros for a bar of chocolate, I can also see why someone might pay 50 cents. It’s still chocolate. And it’s the same product.
The lesson here is twofold: First, you can’t put a price on taste. If you love something, you’ll gladly pay more for a better version of it. Second, if you’re selling a commodity, it’s hard to charge a premium for it. It’s still chocolate. It’s still coffee. It’s still a T-shirt.
There’s a saying that “you can’t polish a turd.” It’s true. But you can also only put so much glitter on gold. Be careful what you sell, and be careful what you buy.

### Title: Nourishing in Increments

### Content: 
One theme in Samurai Champloo is hunger. The protagonist, a teenage girl named Fuu, and her companions—two bickering swordsmen—are mainly trying to make it from meal to meal in feudal Japan.
In Fuu often complains about her growling stomach. She’ll get angry when her two male companions try to eat without her, and she’ll also get angry when they don’t seem to take her hunger as seriously as she does.
Fuu’s hunger is a constant, and she is always trying to satisfy it. The two men, on the other hand, are more accustomed to long periods without food. They’ll sometimes joke about Fuu’s complaints, but they’ll also make do with less, eating only when food is available.
The show offers a lesson about nourishment: If you’re hungry in increments, you’ll get angry in increments. If you accept hunger as a given, you can nourish yourself in increments, and you’ll stay calm.
The same applies to money, relationships, and any other kind of hunger. You can be constantly worried about your next dollar, your next date, or your next compliment, or you can accept that you’ll always be nourished in increments.
It’s okay to be hungry. The question is will you get angry?

In early 1965, Bruce Lee’s father died. He was summoned to Hong Kong to attend the funeral and deal with the estate.
The’t mind the trip. He had been in the United States for seven years, and he was happy to go home for a while.
What he didn’t expect was the barrage of questions from his friends and family about his plans. “When are you coming back to Hong Kong for good?” they asked. “How long are you staying in America?”
At 24 years old, Bruce had no idea. He was still a student. He was working as a waiter. He had no job prospects, no wife, no children. He had no clue what he was going to do with his life, and he wasn’t about to pretend otherwise.
“I don’t know,” he told them. “I’ll just let things happen.”
For the next 48 hours, Bruce was bombarded with the same question over and over again. “What are your plans? What are your plans?”
Finally, he couldn’t take it anymore. He went back to his hotel room, sat down at the desk, and wrote a letter to himself.
“I, Bruce Lee, will be the first highest paid Oriental super star in the United States,” he wrote. “In return, I will give the most exciting performances and render the best of quality in the capacity of an actor. Starting 1970, I will have amassed a fortune of $10,000,000. I will live the way I please and achieve inner harmony and happiness.”
Bruce was not a man of superstition. He didn’t believe in fate. He believed in hard work. But he did believe in using his judgment. He believed in taking a stand and then working towards that stand until he could no longer stand.
“I’m not so sure I can do all those things,” he wrote. “But I’m going to try. I’m going to try damn hard.”
Bruce Lee was not a man who would let things happen. He was a man who made things happen. And so, in 1970, he became the first highest paid Asian actor in Hollywood. In 1971, he became a millionaire. In 1973, he became the most famous martial artist in the world. And in 1973, he died.
